item.title: Meta’s Laptop Surveillance Leak Damages Internal Trust
item.dc:creator: David Geer
item.description: MCI telemetry software logged personal messages, password fields, non-work applications, and sensitive financial activity.
item.content:encoded:
One approach to training agentic AI is eroding workplace privacy and trust: developers are deploying desktop tracking tools that record live screen content, mouse movements, and keystrokes. While designed to learn user workflows, the logging captures passwords, login tokens, and private messages. Installing these tools without clear policies or employee consent adds to workplace friction and creates data security risks.

Meta employees discovered the company was logging their corporate laptops to train internal AI models, according to media reports. Launched in April 2026 under Meta’s Model Capability Initiative (MCI), the software recorded desktop activity of laptops across the U.S. A month later, growing internal backlash led more than 1,600 employees to sign a petition protesting the non-consensual surveillance. In a minor concession in June, Meta executives offered employees the ability to pause tracking for up to thirty minutes at a time. However, later that month, internal monitors uncovered a security incident in which unencrypted MCI telemetry streams were written directly into 45,000 internal Apache Hive database tables company-wide, without role-based access controls. The exposed records were accessible in plain text by employees with database query access. The records included performance reviews, raw AI prompts, and employee chat logs. The exposure forced executives to halt the project indefinitely.

Meta confirmed that the 45,000 Hive tables served as the central storage warehouse for raw plain-text behavior logs. Meta’s proprietary MCI agent captured OS-level framebuffer snapshots and keystrokes on macOS and Windows devices, streaming the data through internal telemetry aggregators directly into Apache Hive storage formats like ORC and Parquet. While Meta intended for these dataset feeds to train autonomous workflow agents, engineers failed to implement data sanitization, token redaction, or access-control tagging before ingestion. Cross-border communications on monitored U.S. laptops pulled international staff and European Union residents into unencrypted domestic datasets, triggering significant GDPR compliance concerns.

Following the leak disclosure, Meta issued a statement: “We have carefully designed this program with privacy safeguards and while we have no indication at this time that any data was improperly accessed by Meta employees, we’re pausing it while we investigate.”

While Meta maintained it had contained exposure internally and that deactivating the background agent across all corporate laptops would take several days, the statement failed to address why they omitted basic data classification standards from the ingestion pipeline in the first place.

No Employee Consent, No Clear Data Usage Limits

In leaked internal memos and in information shared with the news media, Meta leadership claimed MCI telemetry would strictly serve model training and never feed performance evaluations. Yet the software operated without technical boundaries, logging personal messaging, password fields, non-work applications, and sensitive financial activity.

David Redekop, chief executive officer at ADAMnetworks, a cybersecurity company, said there’s a premium on real-world training data because organizations have already trained and retrained AI iteratively on historical, conventionally available datasets.

As frontier AI labs reach saturation on public Web scrapes and synthetic data, high-density human behavioral telemetry, capturing how experts navigate complex desktop environments, has become a new frontier for agentic AI training data.

Redekop called AI model development a kind of arms race and said that any company with internal, fresh data would be tempted to use it. In addition, corporate devices are company-owned, which would technically suffice as a reason to access without employee consent.

For systems architects, this highlights a critical gap in corporate governance: hardware ownership does not automatically grant the authority to bypass zero-trust data classification policies or to collect application-layer secrets without audit logging.

Raw Keystrokes, Private Messages Sit On Accessible Hive Tables

Available information suggests the collection of raw keystrokes and private messages was not a technical error. Rather, it appears to have been an intentional capability of the Model Capability Initiative (MCI), which had the purpose of capturing desktop activities, including application usage, prompts, messages, and potentially keystrokes, for AI model development, said Gail-Joon Ahn, a Fellow of both IEEE and ACM and a professor in the School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence at Arizona State University.

In system design, when organizations engineer endpoint agents with full OS-level hook capabilities such as framebuffer snapshots and keylogging, the security posture depends entirely on downstream pipeline controls rather than endpoint collection limits. Said Ahn, “The technical issue appears to be the subsequent exposure of that collected data due to a system misconfiguration. Without access to Meta’s internal incident report, audit logs, or compliance documentation, it is impossible to identify the exact root cause.”

For software engineers, this underscores the necessity of automated CI/CD schema validation and mandatory role-based access control tagging before central data lakes like Apache Hive ingest raw endpoint streams.

Privacy Reviews Approve Content Capture From Non-U.S. Employees

According to Redekop, organizations frequently attempt to exploit jurisdictional boundaries by restricting the installation of tracking software to U.S.-based hardware. But it creates a compliance blind spot in which foreign employees communicate from monitored U.S. laptops, and cross-border data streams take GDPR-protected communications into domestic data lakes that lack strict privacy controls.

From a regulatory standpoint, relying on hardware deployment geography fails under international privacy law. European data protection authorities such as the European Data Protection Board and privacy advocacy groups like None Of Your Business emphasize that processing non-U.S. personal data in plain-text domestic data lakes, such as the interactions of U.S. workers with EU staff, violates the GDPR.

Local Data Anonymization Not Applied To Laptops

“Mitigating AI training data risk requires strict validation across the data pipeline,” said Brian Walsh, incident response manager at Varonis and FBI cybercrime expert emeritus. Walsh noted that organizations must evaluate whether endpoint tools support client-side masking, anonymization, or filtering scripts before transmitting screen captures to central servers. “If local sanitization isn’t technically supported at collection, organizations are forced to execute rigorous post-collection review and masking. Without strict validation at either stage, collecting sensitive and irrelevant data becomes an inevitability.”

From an engineering standpoint, applying local regex filters or client-side redaction hooks before network egress is computationally lightweight and remains the primary defense against turning central data lakes into liability surfaces.

Monitoring Employees Affects Workplace Trust

“Deploying covert surveillance tools during a wave of corporate layoffs burns through organizational trust at the exact moment it is most fragile,” said Eric R. Burgess, CEO of Credtent, a licensing platform that connects AI companies and content creators. Burgess said profitable tech firms that conduct workforce reductions while installing endpoint tracking software can create insider threats. Companies that treat employees as disposable optimization targets can incentivize frustrated workers to expose internal missteps and leak corporate data, he said.

Meta reportedly conducted sweeping workforce reductions in 2026 while simultaneously rolling out and operating its MCI laptop-tracking software.

The situation highlights the human dimension of insider risk when organizations pair workplace surveillance with workforce reductions: technical security controls can be undermined by eroded employee trust.

Standards To Protect Employee Data Rights

Building and training in-house AI models on employee behavioral telemetry intersects directly with binding legal regulations and international governance standards. In Europe, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689) explicitly classifies AI systems deployed for workplace monitoring and employment decision-making as “high-risk,” imposing strict advance-notice requirements on employers. This operates alongside GDPR Article 35, which mandates a formal Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and strict purpose limitation before an enterprise can repurpose raw employee computer activity into machine learning training pipelines.

In the U.S. and globally, voluntary technical frameworks set the benchmark for enterprise compliance. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) provides systems architects with actionable guidelines for mapping, measuring, and managing human rights risks during data ingestion. Globally, the ISO/IEC 42001 Standard establishes the baseline for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, requiring formalized governance for data provenance, transparency, and data-subject rights whenever harvesting internal corporate datasets.

David Geer is a journalist who focuses on issues related to cybersecurity. He writes from Cleveland, OH, USA.

item.title: Quantum is Gaining, but Don’t Throw Away that Supercomputer
item.dc:creator: Mark Halper
item.description: Quantum computers can deliver staggering compute power but have limitations compared to conventional systems.
item.content:encoded:
When IBM announced in May that two of its quantum computers helped Cleveland Clinic achieve a record-size simulation of human proteins, a couple of other pieces of hardware also stood out in the accomplishment: two supercomputers.

This pairing of quantum computing and classical computing illustrates that while quantum computers can deliver staggering compute power in certain circumstances, they also have limitations compared to conventional systems, which have faster clock rates, established algorithms, are more capable with large datasets, and are more broadly useful than niche-oriented quantum.

“There’s going to be a classical computer in anything that has to do with quantum,” said IBM vice president of quantum adoption Scott Crowder.

There’s plenty of similar thinking around the quantum computing industry, which is routinely partnering with classical high-performance computing (HPC) companies to serve what Marcus Henning, chief business officer of German quantum computing company planqc GmbH, referred to as a “coprocessor” boost to supercomputers. In March, planqc entered an arrangement with end user partners Infineon and BMW to help them combine quantum and supercomputing processes.

The growing list of such partnerships includes a July announcement by quantum company Quantinuum, Rolls-Royce, and the U.K. National Supercomputing Centre at the University of Edinburgh to examine how the combination of quantum and classical computing can improve gas turbine engines. The same month, quantum vendor Rigetti Computing said it will work with supercomputing provider Hewlett Packard Enterprises at the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center to integrate the two technologies. Quantinuum also formed an alliance with HPE in June. IBM has several quantum/classical partnerships in addition to the one with Cleveland Clinic.

A Super Assistant

Quantum computing has been exciting the computing world with eye-popping achievements. One example came in 2024, when a Google quantum computer ran a benchmark algorithm in less than five minutes that the company said would have taken a supercomputer a septillion years. In July of this year, IBM, working with the University of Chicago, announced that its quantum computer had solved in 15 minutes a problem that would “demand infeasible amounts of classical computing time.”

Despite all this brawn, quantum computing is working essentially as a powerful assistant to classical supercomputing, rather than as a replacement.

Why? While quantum is still a work in progress—quantum computing developers are focused on increasing the qubit count in their machines—the answer lies largely in quantum’s reliance on specific algorithms written to solve very specific tasks by taking advantage of quantum properties. Qubits, or quantum bits, can represent zero and one at the same time, a quantum characteristic known as superposition. And they work in conjunction with other qubits, via a quantum process called entanglement.

The combination of superposition and entanglement is what gives quantum computing its enormous computational capabilities.

It’s All About the Algorithms

Yet that is only true if the quantum computer has the proper algorithms. “Quantum is not a general-purpose machine,” said Henning of planqc. “It’s a coprocessor. It solves certain kinds of problems where classical computers are really, really bad. You load it with problems that a classical cannot solve.”

No one is throwing away their classical iron.

“We will still have supercomputers, classical computers, and they’ll have additional tools for different kinds of problems,” Henning said. “One tool will be a quantum computer. With quantum computers, you’re still at the stage where you still have to develop algorithms. With classical computers, we have many, many years of experience. We have very well established algorithms and libraries and codes and all these things.”

So classical computers will continue to carry the general computing workload, probably for a long time to come. Quantum computers won’t supplant them any time soon for AI, for example, because for now, quantum cannot readily absorb large amounts of data. Quantum computers, however, can feed their findings into a classically-driven AI process.

Quantum for Quantum

One of several promising areas for quantum is the simulation of matter, fluid dynamics, physical processes and chemistry. That’s because the quantum properties of quantum computers can echo the quantum makeup of matter which, many physicists believe, exhibit quantum superposition and entangled behavior on the atomic and subatomic level. Thus, quantum computing portends major improvements in materials for batteries, in pharmaceuticals, in aerospace fuel use (as with Quantinuum and Rolls-Royce’s arrangement), and other things.

“You can try to do it classically, but the compute resources you have will never be sufficient for that,” said Henning.

In hybrid projects, quantum hands over its results to a supercomputer for broader application.

That’s what happened when Cleveland Clinic used two IBM quantum computers and two Japanese supercomputers provided through a partnership with Japan’s government-owned research institute RIKEN when it was trying to simulate a couple of human proteins. The combination was able to model two different molecules (one that’s part of the human digestion system, and another that’s part of the human immune system) at a size of 12,635 atoms and11,608 atoms, both roughly 40 times the size of the previous high of 303 atoms.

IBM described the approach as quantum-centric supercomputing. Basically, “Classical broke up the problem into fragments, quantum simulated the pieces” and “classical stitched it back together to get the full answer,” explained IBM’s Crowder.

Quantum/classical combinations also help companies optimize financial portfolios and logistics. For example, planqc’s project with Infineon and BMW aims to optimize supply chain processes. IBM in May announced that it is working with insurance company Allstate to improve its combination of risks and values. To evaluate home insurance policy offerings, IBM’s Heron quantum computer “generates a batch of candidate answers nudged toward combinations that are both valuable and within budget,” an IBM representative said. “Then, a classical step cleans up the list.”

“Quantum computers are a very niche tool for very important problems which currently you can’t even approach on a classical computer,” said Mykola Maksymenko, co-founder and chief technology officer of New York City-based Haiqu, which simulates quantum processes on classical computers.

Analog, or Nature’s Way

One irony is that quantum computers work their “septillion year” wonders even though they are, by the conventional measurement of clock speed, slower than classical systems. While today’s high-performance classical computers run in the terahertz range, a quantum computer might run in the hertz range of one operation per second. That’s one reason they are not good at large data processing.

It’s a striking difference. But clock speed is misleading from the quantum perspective, because quantum doesn’t rely on it. Rather, what is lost in clock speed is made up with the exponential power of combining superposition and entanglement for specific tasks.

Izhar Madalsy, co-founder and CEO of Quantum Elements, Los Angeles, described quantum as a return to the analog world—a notable departure from the digital side of computing to which the world is accustomed.

Quantum computers are analog precisely because the quantum mechanics on which they are based are themselves analog, Madalsy said. “While when you look at quantum devices, which are analog devices, they’re very good at representing complex systems that are rooted in quantum physics,” he said. “They represent nature using an analog system.”

In short, he said, quantum computing “is an analog beast.”

Mark Halper is a freelance journalist based near Bristol, U.K. He covers everything from media moguls to subatomic particles.

item.title: Two Ways Into the Maze: From Bidirectional BFS to Bidirectional Dijkstra
item.dc:creator: Sai Charan Obuladinne
item.description: Route planners' problems are that roads have travel times, tolls, or traffic, and their goal is the cheapest trip, not the one with the fewest turns.
item.content:encoded:
This fall, my family and I walked into a maze built from stacked hay bales, with pumpkins along the edges and kids racing through every passage. We didn’t stay together. Half of us went in through one entrance, and the other half went in through the opposite one. Nobody drew a map. Each group simply tried the next opening, and after a few turns we heard each other’s voices and met somewhere in the middle. Once we met, we knew the whole way through.

Two Groups, One Search

Without planning it, we had acted out one of the most useful ideas in computer science: search from both ends at once. In a maze every step costs the same, and the standard way to explore it is breadth-first search, or BFS. You check every spot one step away, then every spot two steps away, and so on. Run that from both entrances and you get bidirectional BFS: two waves of searching that meet in the middle.

Why bother with two groups? Because searches grow quickly. If every spot leads to three new ones and the exit is ten steps away, one group might check around 59,000 spots. Two groups that each go only five steps check about 500 between them. Splitting the distance in half doesn’t halve the work; it shrinks it dramatically.

When Steps Stop Being Equal

A hay maze is a friendly world, because every step is equal. Real problems rarely are. Picture a map of towns instead of hay passages, where every town charges a toll to pass through. Now the question isn’t “what’s the shortest walk?” but “what’s the cheapest trip?” A route through two expensive towns can cost more than a route through four cheap ones, and BFS, which only counts steps, can’t tell the difference.

Dijkstra, From Both Ends

The tool for costs is Dijkstra’s algorithm. Instead of exploring by step count, it always moves to the cheapest place it can reach next. One small trick fits this map: entering a town costs that town’s toll, so the tolls on the towns become costs on the roads leading into them. C costs 2, D costs 5, E costs 3, and so on.

Now bring back the two groups. One search starts at A and moves forward, always taking the cheapest next town. The other starts at Z and moves backward the same way. Just as in the maze, each side only has to cover about half the map before they meet.

Let’s watch it happen on the map. Each town’s number is what you pay to enter it, and each search keeps a running total.

1.) The search from A looks at its neighbors first: C costs 2, E costs 3, and B costs 4.

2.) The search from Z does the same on its side: W costs 2, X costs 3, and Y costs 4.

3.) Each search takes its cheapest option first. From A, that’s C (2), which leads on to D for a total of 2 + 5 = 7. From Z, it’s W (2), which reaches E for a total of 2 + 3 = 5 and D for 2 + 5 = 7.

4.) Now both searches have touched the same towns. Through E, the route A → E → W → Z costs 3 + 2 = 5. Through D, the route A → C → D → W → Z costs 2 + 5 + 2 = 9. The best so far is 5.

The cheapest step still waiting on A’s side is E (3), and on Z’s side it’s X (3). Together that’s 6, already more than 5, so nothing left can beat the route we have. We stop, and the costly towns on the outer routes, such as B, F, u, Y, and V, never get fully explored

Meeting is Not The Same as Finishing

This is the part that is easy to get wrong. In the maze, the first meeting is the answer. With tolls, it might not be. On this map the two searches can meet along three routes: through D (cost 9), through F and u (cost 10), and through E and W (cost 5). When the searches meet, we remember the cost of that route and keep going. We stop only when the cheapest next step from A plus the cheapest next step from Z already costs at least as much as the best route found. At that point, nothing left can beat it. And the meeting town’s toll is counted once, not once from each side.

Here the winner is A → E → W → Z, at 3 + 2 = 5. On a map this small the savings are tiny, but on road networks or graphs with millions of points, two searches meeting in the middle can be the difference between exploring most of the map and exploring a small piece of it.

This isn’t just a puzzle trick. Route planners face exactly this problem: roads have travel times, tolls, or traffic, and the goal is the cheapest trip, not the one with the fewest turns. Searching from both the start and the destination is a well-known way to speed that up on huge road maps. The same idea works for network routing, where each link has a delay, and for any problem with a clear start, a clear goal, and a cost for every step.

That afternoon in the maze, two groups and a few shouts were enough to find the way. Real systems need one more rule: don’t just meet in the middle, make sure you have met on the cheapest path.

Disclosure: AI tools were used for research assistance, reference gathering, and editorial support in preparing this article.

References

1. Dijkstra, E.W. A note on two problems in connexion with graphs, Numerische Mathematik 1 (1959), pp. 269–271.

2. Pohl, I. Bi-directional Search, Machine Intelligence 6 (1971), pp. 127–140.

3. Bidirectional search, Wikipedia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bidirectional_search

Sai Charan Obuladinne is a Staff Engineering Manager at GEICO, where he drives strategic technical initiatives for claims platforms in close collaboration with ML teams. Previously, he was a Staff Software Engineer at Meta, and he has spent over a decade building back-end systems across advertising, healthcare, and logistics.

item.title: Orchestration: From Personal Sound Signature to Personal Computation Signature
item.dc:creator: Orit Wolf
item.description: Orchestration seeks to coordinate autonomous musical and computational entities so that their collective intelligence exceeds the capabilities of any individual component.
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever wondered about the origin of the term orchestration, which has recently gained widespread attention with the rapid growth of agentic software development?

Orchestration is traditionally defined as the art and science of assigning musical ideas to instruments. Yet this definition captures only part of its significance. Drawing on contemporary scholarship, we understand orchestration here as the intentional coordination of distinct musical voices into a coherent expressive whole.4,6 Rather than asking simply which instrument should play a given passage, orchestration addresses the broader question of how specialized voices can interact to create musical meaning that transcends their individual contributions. In this sense, orchestration is the process of organizing individual capabilities, timbres, and musical functions so the whole becomes greater than the sum of its parts.

Historically, the need for orchestration evolved alongside the development of the modern orchestra. During the Renaissance and Baroque periods, instruments served both to reinforce vocal writing and to participate in increasingly independent instrumental genres, with instrumental color acquiring different roles across musical contexts.10 As orchestras expanded during the Classical period, composers such as Haydn and Mozart gradually established increasingly differentiated roles for instrumental families.3 By the nineteenth century, larger concert halls, advances in instrument construction, and the growing expressive ambitions of Romantic composers transformed orchestration into an artistic discipline in its own right.1,9

Hector Berlioz’s Grand traité d’instrumentation et d’orchestration modernes (1844) is widely recognized as one of the most influential treatises on instrumentation and orchestration. Berlioz described the orchestra not as a collection of separate instruments, but as a single large instrument capable of producing an almost limitless spectrum of expressive possibilities.2 This represented a profound conceptual shift. The orchestra itself became the instrument, while individual musicians functioned as specialized yet interdependent contributors within a unified expressive system. Berlioz’s vision laid the foundations for modern orchestral thinking and profoundly influenced later composers and orchestrators.5,9

Several decades later, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov’s Principles of Orchestration (completed after his death by Maximilian Steinberg; first published in Russian in 1913 and in English in 1922) further advanced this perspective by emphasizing not only the characteristics of individual instruments but, more importantly, their interaction, balance, transparency, and collective function.6,8 Successful orchestration emerged not from the excellence of isolated parts, but from the quality of their relationships. Later orchestration scholars have argued that orchestration is best understood as the design of meaningful interactions between musical voices, rather than simply the accumulation of instrumental colors.1,4

Yet orchestration does more than coordination. It is also one of the primary ways in which composers establish an individual artistic identity. Two composers, or even two orchestrators, may begin with the same melody, harmony, instrumentation, and formal design, yet produce profoundly different sonic experiences. Their choices in timbre, register, density, spacing, articulation, balance, and interaction create a musical voice listeners often recognize almost immediately. Maurice Ravel’s orchestration of Mussorgsky’s Pictures at an Exhibition is perhaps the best-known demonstration that orchestration can fundamentally reshape the perception and expressive meaning of musical material.7

Musical Orchestration: Personal Sound Signature

Building upon this observation, we introduce the concept of a Personal Sound Signature (PSS): the distinctive sonic identity that emerges through recurring orchestration decisions. A PSS is not determined by the instruments themselves, but by the way instruments are organized, combined, layered, balanced, and allowed to interact. In this sense, orchestration is simultaneously a process of coordination and an act of authorship. It reveals the orchestrator’s aesthetic values, artistic priorities, interpretive judgement, and creative imagination. The same musical resources can therefore generate entirely different artistic worlds because orchestration reflects the orchestrator’s identity as much as the orchestra’s capabilities.

From this perspective, orchestration fulfills two inseparable functions. First, it coordinates specialized musical agents into a coherent expressive system. Second, it constructs a distinctive sonic identity through the particular manner in which those agents are coordinated. Orchestration is therefore both functional and expressive: it organizes complexity while simultaneously creating uniqueness.

Building upon this historical tradition, we propose that orchestration may be understood more broadly as a general principle of coordinated intelligence. Rather than viewing orchestration solely as a compositional technique, it can be conceptualized as the organization of specialized agents into a coherent system capable of producing outcomes that exceed the capacities of its individual components. Under this framework, diversity is not an obstacle, but a prerequisite for collective intelligence. Each participant contributes distinct capabilities while operating within a shared structure of communication, timing, responsibility, and purpose. The coherence of the system emerges from the intelligent coordination of difference.

Remarkably, this broader conception extends well beyond the concert hall. Nearly two centuries after Berlioz articulated the orchestra as an integrated system of specialized yet interdependent voices, computer scientists adopted the concept of orchestration to address a strikingly similar challenge in distributed and multi-agent systems. Although separated by domain and technology, both musical and computational orchestration seek to answer the same fundamental question: How can specialized, autonomous entities be coordinated so that their collective intelligence exceeds the capabilities of any individual component?

In this post, we argue that music contributes an additional and largely unexplored dimension to this discussion. Beyond coordination, orchestration also shapes identity. Just as composers develop a Personal Sound Signature through the way they organize musical resources, designers of multi-agent systems may likewise create distinctive orchestration strategies that reflect particular priorities, values, and modes of interaction. The true power of orchestration, whether musical or computational, lies in transforming coordination itself into a unique and recognizable signature of intelligence, rather than only in coordinating specialized entities.

Orchestration: From Coordinated Programs to Agentic Intelligence

Orchestration is traditionally understood in computing as the coordination and management of multiple computational processes, services, or components so they operate together toward a common objective. Yet this definition captures only part of its significance. In agentic programming, orchestration increasingly involves intentionally coordinating distinct agents, tools, processes, and sources of knowledge into a coherent intelligent system. Rather than simply asking which agent should perform a given task, orchestration addresses the broader question of how specialized agents can interact, communicate, reason, and act to produce outcomes that transcend their individual capabilities. In this sense, orchestration is the process of organizing individual capabilities, roles, knowledge sources, and actions so the whole becomes greater than the sum of its parts.

Historically, the need for orchestration in computing emerged as software systems grew more complex. Early programs were largely conceived as sequences of explicitly specified instructions executed by a single computational process. As software systems grew in scale, developers increasingly decomposed them into modules, procedures, objects, services, and distributed components, each responsible for a specialized function. Software engineering paradigms such as structured programming, object-oriented programming, component-based development, and service-oriented architectures progressively shifted attention from individual instructions toward the organization and interaction of computational entities. The challenge was no longer just implementing an individual function, but coordinating multiple specialized components so they could collectively accomplish a larger computational purpose.

The emergence of distributed computing and workflow systems further established orchestration as a central computational concern. Complex applications came to involve multiple services, data sources, execution environments, and computational processes that had to be coordinated in a particular sequence or according to particular dependencies. Workflow engines and cloud-computing platforms subsequently made orchestration an explicit layer of system design: developers specified how specialized computational components should be invoked, combined, monitored, and integrated, rather than implementing every operation as a monolithic process. The system itself increasingly became the object of design, while its individual components served as specialized yet interdependent contributors within a larger computational architecture.

The emergence of AI agents introduces a profound extension of this trajectory. Traditional software orchestration generally coordinates components whose behavior is largely specified in advance. Agentic systems, by contrast, incorporate entities that can interpret goals, reason about possible actions, select tools, adapt their behavior, and respond to changing environments. An agent may therefore determine not only what operation to perform, but also how to pursue an objective within a given set of constraints and resources. This introduces a fundamental shift in the nature of orchestration. The orchestrator no longer coordinates only predefined computational steps; it coordinates entities that themselves possess a degree of autonomy.

This distinction is particularly important in multi-agent and agentic programming systems. A complex task may be decomposed among a planner agent, a research agent, a coding agent, a testing agent, and a critic agent, with each agent contributing a different capability. The orchestrator determines which agents to select, when to invoke them, what information they receive, how they communicate outputs to other agents, and how to evaluate and integrate intermediate results. And, as in the case of musical orchestration, successful orchestration therefore emerges from the quality of the relationships among agents, rather than from the excellence of isolated agents. A highly capable collection of agents can nevertheless produce poor results if their roles overlap, their communication is inadequate, their outputs are not critically evaluated, or their activities are poorly sequenced.

Building upon the historical development of software orchestration, we propose that orchestration may be understood more broadly as a general principle of agentic intelligence. Rather than viewing orchestration solely as a technical mechanism for managing multiple agents, it can be conceptualized as the organization of specialized autonomous entities into a coherent system capable of producing outcomes that exceed the capabilities of its individual components. Each agent contributes distinct capabilities while operating within a shared structure of communication, timing, responsibility, constraints, and purpose.

Yet orchestration does more than coordination. It is also one of the primary ways in which developers establish the identity and character of an agentic system. Two developers, or two development teams, may employ the same underlying language model, the same tools, the same collection of agents, and even the same overall task, yet produce profoundly different system behaviors. Their choices regarding decomposition, role assignment, delegation, communication, memory, tool selection, sequencing, verification, feedback, and intervention generate different forms of agentic intelligence. One system may emphasize autonomy and exploration; another may privilege verification and control. One may rely on iterative critique; another may employ parallel specialized agents. The resulting behavior is therefore shaped not only by the capabilities of the underlying agents, but by the way those capabilities are orchestrated.

Agentic Orchestration: Personal Computation Signature

Building on this analogy with musical orchestration, Personal Computation Signature (PCS) can be interpreted as the distinctive pattern of agentic behavior that emerges through recurring orchestration decisions made by a developer or development team. A PCS is determined by how agents and tools are organized, combined, delegated, sequenced, monitored, and allowed to interact. Two developers can therefore use identical computational resources while creating systems that behave differently because they orchestrate those resources differently. In this sense, orchestration is simultaneously a process of coordination and an act of authorship. It reveals not only technical expertise but also design priorities, epistemic assumptions, risk tolerance, desired levels of autonomy, and a philosophy of human-AI collaboration.

From this perspective, orchestration fulfills two inseparable functions. First, it coordinates specialized computational agents into a coherent intelligent system. Second, it constructs a distinctive agentic identity through the particular manner in which those agents are coordinated. Therefore, as in the case of musical orchestration, orchestration is both functional and expressive: it organizes computational complexity while simultaneously creating a distinctive mode of intelligence.

This perspective also distinguishes agentic orchestration from traditional program composition. In conventional programming, the developer specifies the computational procedure: the sequence of operations through which the system transforms inputs into outputs. In agentic programming, the developer increasingly specifies goals, constraints, capabilities, roles, and relationships, while allowing agents to determine some of the intermediate steps required to achieve the desired outcome. The programmer therefore moves from specifying every computational action toward designing the cognitive architecture and orchestration structure within which autonomous entities can reason and act. Orchestration consequently becomes a central programming activity rather than merely an infrastructure concern.

Musical Orchestration and Agentic Orchestration

Remarkably, this development brings computing conceptually closer to music. Just as the orchestra transforms individual instruments into a coordinated expressive system, an agentic system transforms individual agents, tools, and knowledge resources into a coordinated intelligent system. In both cases, the central design challenge is not simply to maximize the capability of individual components, but to determine how specialized entities should be organized so that their interactions generate capabilities that no individual component possesses on its own. The orchestrator, like the conductor or composer, therefore operates at a level above the individual contributors, shaping their roles, relationships, timing, and collective behavior.

Just as composers develop a Personal Sound Signature through the way they organize musical resources, developers of agentic systems may develop a Personal Computation Signature through the way they organize computational resources, agents, tools, and interactions. That is, the true power of orchestration, whether musical or computational, lies in transforming coordination itself into a distinctive and recognizable signature of intelligence.

References

1. Adler, S. The Study of Orchestration (3rd ed.). W. W. Norton (2002).

2. Berlioz, H. Berlioz’s orchestration treatise: A translation and commentary (H. Macdonald, Trans. & Ed.). Cambridge University Press (2002).

item.title: Synergizing LLMs and Formal Methods for Neural-Symbolic Reasoning
item.dc:creator: Jin Song Dong
item.description: Presenting a neural-symbolic paradigm in which LLMs propose candidate artifacts and formal methods gate acceptance with machine-checkable certificates.
item.content:encoded:
In recent years, the rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has marked a transformative shift in the landscape of artificial intelligence and many of its applications: software engineering,12 finance,28 healthcare,13 and legal,14 among others. Top LLMs, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek, have demonstrated impressive capabilities in multimodal understanding, generation, coding, task execution, and reasoning. Leveraging these capabilities, agentic LLMs can plan, take actions, and use feedback loops with memory to achieve goals autonomously.

Key Insights

  • LLMs can lower the entry barrier to formal methods (FM) by helping users express informal requirements, generate candidate artifacts, and interact with formal tools.

  • LLMs explore the design space by proposing candidate artifacts, while FM back ends enforce a certificate-based acceptance boundary grounded in explicit assurance targets.

  • A promising direction is to unify these paradigms by using LLMs for generation and interaction, while relying on FM to enforce correctness and interpretability.

  • The aim of an LLM+FM architecture is not merely to produce better average outputs, but to make success and failure observable through formal feedback, with completion gated by a certificate.

Despite these advances, LLM reasoning suffers from a fundamental limitation: the tendency to produce factually incorrect or logically inconsistent yet plausible outputs, commonly termed hallucinations.11 This poses serious risks in high-stakes domains, where trustworthiness is critical. Importantly, this issue is not anomalous but rather mathematically inherent to the probabilistic objectives underlying LLM training. As an example, we asked the LLMs to solve a simple puzzle: In 318, only one digit is correct, and it is in the correct position. In 379, only one digit is correct, but it is in the wrong position. In 863, two digits are correct, but they are in the wrong positions. In 421, no digits are correct. What’s the correct combination of the three digits and their positions? Older models such as GPT 4.1, Gemini 2.5, Claude 4 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3, and Grok 3 gave wrong answers with believable thinking processes. Reasoning models, such as the “Thinking” or “Pro” modes, fared better but took minutes to respond. Small open source LLMs performed poorly and often fell into an infinite loop of reasoning. These models are constantly evolving—the latest versions of GPT, Gemini, and Claude all answered correctly (698). However, hallucinations persist, and theoretically cannot be eradicated by training better LLMs alone.26

Interestingly, we also asked Claude 4 to translate the puzzle into Z3’s SMT-LIB format, which Z3 solved correctly in 0.01 seconds on a laptop (MacBook Pro with M1 Pro). Z3 is a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver,7 offering rigorous reasoning complementary to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. More broadly, formal methods (FM) provide mathematically precise tools for trustworthy computing: SMT extends classical satisfiability to theories such as arithmetic, bit-vectors, arrays, datatypes, and uninterpreted functions; theorem proving derives valid formulas from axioms via proof calculi; and model checking systematically explores system states to detect property violations.

Compared to the uncertain and generative nature of LLMs, formal methods deliver rigorous correctness guarantees, but their adoption is limited by steep learning curves and high expertise requirements. A promising direction is to unify these paradigms by leveraging LLMs for generation and interaction while using formal methods to enforce correctness and interpretability.6,25

A Neural-Symbolic Reasoning Paradigm

Notable neural-symbolic AI methods.  A common early pattern in LLM-based formal reasoning is loosely coupled integration, where an LLM translates a problem into a formal language for a symbolic solver, and solver failures due to syntactic or semantic issues are fed back to the LLM for iterative refinement.2,19,21 In contrast, tightly integrated approaches embed neural reasoning directly into the formal reasoning loop. For example, LeanDojo employs retrieval-augmented premise selection based on the current proof state and an encoder-decoder transformer to propose the next proof tactic, enabling fine-grained neural-symbolic collaboration.27

Other tightly integrated paradigms include logical neural networks (LNNs), where neurons correspond to components of weighted logical formulas in a real-valued logic, yielding end-to-end differentiability, omnidirectional inference, and training-time enforcement of logical consistency.20 Scallop further advances this line through a neurosymbolic programming language and compiler that supports data- and computation-efficient training while delivering strong performance, interpretability, and generalization across diverse tasks.15 Beyond such architectures, directly integrating formal methods into the internal components of LLMs remains possible but prohibitively resource intensive. Our work instead adopts a practical and complementary strategy: constraining, checking, and guiding LLM outputs via external formal methods without requiring access to model internals. By formalizing the representations, constraints, and reasoning interfaces between LLMs and downstream systems, we ensure verifiability while enabling accessible deployment of reliability mechanisms in high-stakes applications.

Our paradigm.  Across integration styles, common neural-symbolic interaction themes emerge (Figure 1). To lower the entry barrier, natural language is used as input, with multiple LLM agents coordinated by an agentic task automation LLM that selects agents, interacts with users, and automates the workflow. Complex problems typically follow a “plan-execute” decomposition.12 The resulting gap between informal input and formal specifications is bridged by an autoformalization LLM, while a designing LLM converts underspecified prompts into high-level designs. Given the close link between formal methods and software engineering, many execution steps involve programming and are handled by a coding LLM. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies domain knowledge, including language syntax and semantics, and enables downstream applications. LLM agents interact with formal reasoning engines, including SMT solvers, theorem provers, and model checkers, whose reliable outputs provide high-quality feedback for repairing and refining autoformalized code.

Guidelines on architecture design.  An LLM+FM architecture should be selected from the assurance target outward, rather than from an LLM workflow inward. The aim is not merely better average outputs, but rather an architecture where success and failure are observable through formal feedback and where completion is gated by a certificate, that is, machine-checkable evidence produced by the FM back end (e.g., a localized conflict explanation, a violating execution trace, or an undischarged proof). This also future-proofs the design: LLM capabilities may change quickly, but the acceptance boundary is defined by certificates that can be validated independently of the LLM.

Design Rule 1 (Assurance target).  State the artifact that must be correct and the related properties that define correctness. Write the acceptance claim in the form “This output is acceptable because <property> holds for <artifact>.” If this claim cannot be stated precisely, later choices drift toward optimizing fluency or convenience rather than the intended notion of correctness.

Design Rule 2 (Back-end FM choice).  An FM back end should be chosen to match the property class and, more fundamentally, the domain of quantification. For constraint satisfiability and consistency questions that expect definitive outcomes (e.g., SAT/UNSAT), SMT-based back ends are most appropriate, as they determine logical formula satisfiability and can return unsat cores to localize conflicting constraints, providing constraint-level correctness. For behavioral and temporal properties, model checking is better suited, as it reasons exhaustively over transition systems, verifies whether all executions satisfy a temporal specification, and otherwise produces counterexample traces, with first-class support for safety, liveness, and fairness, yielding behavioral/temporal correctness. For refinement and high-assurance correctness, theorem proving and refinement checking adopt a proof-centric approach, generating and discharging proof obligations to certify that a system meets its specification by construction, providing semantic, unbounded correctness; when full certification is too costly, lighter-weight techniques such as type systems, abstract interpretation, or contract checking can offer faster but partial guarantees.

Design Rule 3 (LLM-FM interface).  After fixing the FM back end, define the contract between generation and validation by deciding what the LLM may propose (candidates, decompositions, repairs) and what the FM tool must return on failure. Treat formal failures as typed signals rather than generic “try again” events, so prompts and repair logic are organized around channels such as inconsistency, counterexample, or unsatisfied obligation. Finer-grained diagnostics typically shorten repair cycles and reduce silent failure, at the cost of tighter tool integration and more orchestrated iterations. A further trade-off is where human effort is spent: It can be front-loaded via structured inputs that reduce ambiguity, or back-loaded via flexible inputs plus more validation cycles and occasional interactive confirmation.

Design Rule 4 (Integration pattern).  Select a coupling pattern that matches the dominant failure mode and the task abstraction level. For decision/compliance settings (e.g., access-control policies, configuration constraints), consistency-guarded deliberation works well: Deliberate freely, but gate acceptance with a consistency checker that surfaces localized conflicts. For system-level behaviors (e.g., protocol workflows, safety controllers), counterexample-guided refinement is effective: Failed checks yield executions that drive targeted revisions, at the cost of repeated checking and occasional abstraction. For component synthesis (e.g., critical parsers and code), proof-obligation guided synthesis is effective: Obligations pinpoint repair targets, but require precise specifications and manageable proof burden. Patterns are often combined across layers; when both system- and code-level assurance are needed, certify the higher-level model or contracts first, then constrain and certify lower-level synthesis.

Design Rule 5 (Acceptance guard).  State explicitly the certificate that gates acceptance for the end-to-end system and what exactly it certifies. This operationalizes “good vs. bad” choices and makes trade-offs legible: Stronger certificates raise iteration cost and may narrow applicability, while lighter-weight certificates broaden scope but leave more residual uncertainty. In practice, designs are most robust when they align the architecture with the task abstraction level, treat FM as the correctness filter rather than an optional add-on, and keep a clean separation between candidate generation and certificate-based validation.

In summary, LLMs and FM will form a complementary and beneficial generate-validate loop in future applications: LLMs explore the design space by proposing candidate artifacts, while FM back ends enforce a certificate-based acceptance boundary grounded in explicit assurance targets. Formal failures verified by FM would become structured feedback that guides iterative refinement, aligning probabilistic generation with semantic guarantees. In the following sections, we will provide some examples of our neural-symbolic reasoning paradigm to demonstrate the different roles of LLMs and formal reasoning in a variety of application domains.

FM4LLM: Legal AI with LLM-SMT Integration

As our first case study, we show how formal reasoning enhances the reliability and consistency of LLM outputs in legal reasoning. While substantive rationality concerns fairness and morality, formal rationality demands logical adherence to the law. Existing legal LLMs, such as LawLLM,22 primarily rely on natural language processing and retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucinations, but still lack logically grounded and reliable reasoning.

Our approach,4 shown in Figure 2, addresses the above issue using SMT solving. Each statutory clause c is parsed into a typed rule Rule(c):=〈Actor,Action,Cond,Penalty〉, and compiled into a first-order implicationϕc:=∀x.Actor(x)∧Action(x)∧Cond(x)→Penalty(x). All articles form the static legal knowledge base K:={ϕc|c∈Statutes}. Given a case D, the Prosecutor and Attorney LLMs generate (FP,SP):=ProsecutorLLM(D),(FD,SD):=AttorneyLLM(D), where F are fact predicates and S are cited clauses. The autoformalization LLM acts neutrally and takes the evidence provided by the above two LLMs and generates SMT-LIB format formal code that Z3 can check. If Z3 reports unsatisfiable, we will extract the minimal unsatisfiable core, representing the simplest reason that causes logical inconsistency. The autoformalization LLM maps this core back to the original text and instructs the Prosecutor or Attorney LLM to drop the contradictory clauses, then asks Z3 to check for consistency again.

Example.  Consider the following real case: (Gong Qiang concerns a repeat narcotics offender) Defendant Gong Qiang received a WeChat message from Luo, requesting the purchase of 1,000 yuan worth of drugs. After receiving the 1,000 yuan transfer from Luo via WeChat, Gong Qiang delivered 2 grams of methamphetamine and six magu tablets to Luo at approximately 5:00 PM …

Taking the case information as input, the Prosecutor LLM (accusatory stance) extracts:

  • Actors: Defendant Gong Qiang (prior drug convictions), buyer Luo; public prosecution by Donghu District People’s Procuratorate

  • Acts: Sold 2g methamphetamine + 6 “magu” tablets for 1,000 RMB

  • Evidence: WeChat payment record, seized drugs, positive urine tests, confession

  • Aggravators: Repeat drug offender in five-year window; multiple prior administrative penalties

  • Statutory Law: [64, 65]; [347, 356]

On the other hand, the Attorney LLM (exculpatory stance) extracts:

  • Actors: Defendant Gong Qiang, buyer Luo; defense counsel appointed

  • Acts: Acknowledge sale but stress “very small quantity” and no wider circulation

  • Evidence: WeChat record, drug test, confession

  • Mitigators: Full confession, signed plea agreement, voluntary compensation and buyer’s understanding; prior sentence already served, limited social harm

  • Statutory Law: [64, 67]; [347, 356]

The autoformalization LLM analyzes the above results and further extracts the following facts and converts them into SMT-LIB format, then sends them to the Z3 solver together with the extracted rules and clauses:

  • Article 65: matched field { prior_sentence: True, reoffense_in_5_years: True }

  • Article 67: matched field { truthful_confession: True }

  • Article 347: matched fields {subject: person, action: traffic_narcotics, object: narcotics, intent: intentional}

Z3 evaluates the logical constraints and produces consistent results, which a judge LLM converts into a human-readable verdict of two years’ imprisonment and a 10,000 yuan fine, close to the ground truth of one year and two months with an 11,000 yuan penalty. This legally informed integration employs multiple role-specific LLM agents coordinated with an SMT solver to ensure logical consistency, leading to more realistic sentencing and the highest accuracy among state-of-the-art methods.4

LLM4FM: LLM Model-Checking Agent

LLMs can reduce the costly manual effort in formal methods. This case study presents a multi-LLM-agent framework that automates the full model-checking workflow. While model checking itself is automated once a formal model and properties are provided, its industrial adoption is hindered by the manual creation of models and specifications, which requires expertise in checker-specific modeling languages and temporal logics unfamiliar to most engineers.

Autoformalization is central to LLM-driven formal methods. Prior work has used LLMs to translate natural language into linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas9 and to synthesize or repair formal proofs,8 but these do not target system-level modeling. Our case study focuses on the Process Analysis Toolkit (PAT),23 which employs CSP#10 as the modeling language. The PAT-Agent framework29 (Figure 3) takes a natural language system description comprising system behavior and expected properties, translating the former into a formal model and the latter into requirements—properties with specified expected outcomes (i.e., expected to hold or not hold).

We introduce the following notation: Let LNL be the space of natural language descriptions, Π the planning representations, P the generation plans, M the PAT models, Q the user requirements, V PAT’s verification procedure, C the counterexample traces, and R the repair directives. With these notations, our pipeline is summarized by the four transformations:

T plan : L NL → Π → P ; T gen : P → M ; V : M × Q → { MATCH , MISMATCH } m × C ; T repair : M × C × R → M .

Our objective is to obtain a model M*∈M such that ∀(ϕ,o)∈Q:V(M*,ϕ)=o. In the first stage, a Planning LLM parses the system description to extract semantic elements such as constants, variables, actions, and guards, and produces a model-generation plan that defines the intended structure and includes placeholder annotations with explanatory comments to guide subsequent code synthesis. It also processes the user-specified requirements for the system (e.g., reachability and liveness requirements).

User studies show that PAT-Agent translates requirements with 99.6% accuracy across multiple projects. In rare cases, manual checks are still required, supported by optional checkpoints in PAT-Agent. In the second stage, a Coding LLM translates the model-generation plan into CSP# code, guided by formal syntax and semantics and a corpus of existing PAT models. In our experiments, Claude 3.7 Sonnet generates CSP# code with near-perfect syntax on the first attempt, with any minor issues resolved automatically through brief LLM interaction. Full semantic correctness cannot be guaranteed in an automated method, as it depends on user intent, but this issue can be mitigated by checking the generated model against the automatically formalized properties and expected outcomes using PAT. Assuming that the properties are formalized correctly and they sufficiently capture the user’s intent, model checking itself will largely resolve modeling inaccuracies. When mismatches occur, a model repair loop is triggered: PAT’s output, including counterexamples, guides a Repair Agent to identify and fix only the faulty code region rather than regenerating the entire model. In practice, three to four repair iterations typically suffice to satisfy all properties.

Example.  An electrical engineer describes the motor engine as follows:a

This process models a car’s motor. The engine can be turned on and off, the car can start and stop driving, the fuel is gradually consumed after driving, and it can be refueled.

The Planning LLM extracts and defines key constants, variables, and actions (e.g., carMotion, fuel, engineStatus, startDriving), assigning context-appropriate names and inferring implicit system logic using common sense. For example, it deduces that startDriving requires the engine to be on, the car to be stationary, sufficient fuel, and driver presence. The Coding LLM then instantiates this plan by filling in concrete model details, translating such inferred actions into:

[engineStatus == engineOn && carMotion == stop && (fuel > 0)
    && driver == inCar]
startDriving {carMotion = drive;} -> motor()

The code follows CSP# syntax [conditions] event_name data_operations -> next_process(), where guards specify enabling conditions and data operations define event effects, and it passes PAT’s syntax check on the first attempt. The Coding LLM also formalizes system requirements, for example, translating “the car should not be in driving mode without the key” into a reachability assertion, where the state driveWithoutKey is expected to be unreachable:

#define driveWithoutKey (carMotion==drive && key!=inCar);
#assert car reaches driveWithoutKey;     // Expects Invalid

However, verification results may show that the above state is reachable given the initial model generated by the Coding LLM. This issue, together with a counterexample trace composed of system states that lead to the error, is sent to the Repair Agent for a repair iteration, after which the above process is revised as follows to avoid the error:

[engineStatus == engineOn && carMotion == stop && (fuel > 0)
    && driver == inCar
&& key == inCar] startDriving {carMotion = drive;} -> motor()

Interestingly, this issue reflects a real-life situation in which a coauthor of this article kept the engine on and dropped off a passenger, who took the key, at a shopping mall. The author continued to drive the car to the office, only to realize he could not lock the car! With PAT-Agent, automakers can now verify their designs without the excuse of, “But we do not have formal methods engineers.”

They Are One: Trustworthy AI Coder

Some powerful integrations of neural-symbolic reasoning require the two parts to work hand in hand in each small step. This case study demonstrates an AI coder that combines LLMs, program refinement, and theorem proving into a hybrid system. LLMs have shown potent coding capabilities, and the latest ones have raised the bar to the project level—the user only needs to give a one-line prompt, and GPT 5 can build a fully functional website. However, the fundamental reliability problem remains: Is the code functionally correct with respect to user specifications?

Example.  We asked GPT 5 to write the following function: Generate a program that finds the square root of N within the error bound e.

GPT 5 produced the Python code below. However, the reader can check that the two lines after the for loop are incorrect, as there exist N and e such that abs(x_next - x) <= e, but abs(x_next⌃2 - N) > e, which violates the specification. Such issues prompted us to build a reliable AI coder,3 illustrated in Figure 4. To ensure correctness, we adopt the refinement calculus18 to derive code from first-order logic specifications via correctness-preserving transformations. A program is viewed as a predicate transformer, and refinement as logical implications between transformers. Starting from a pure specification Spec, the calculus incrementally replaces conjuncts and quantifiers with executable constructs, such as assignments, guards, loops, and nondeterministic choices using laws like assignment introduction, guard strengthening, and loop introduction, until only code remains. Traditionally, each refinement step requires human intervention:  selecting a refinement law whose side conditions hold, instantiating schema variables to produce a program fragment, and discharging the proof obligations (POs) ensuring Spec⊑Code. This manual workflow scales poorly for real-world systems, where large specifications may require hundreds of refinement steps. To address scalability, we integrate LLMs into the refinement loop. Given the current specification state Si, the LLM predicts a suitable refinement law, instantiates it to generate a candidate code fragment Ci, and emits the associated proof obligation (PO) induced by the refinement law. For example, the VC for an assignment, {P}x:=E{Q}, requires proving the logical implication P⇒Q[x↦E]. An automated theorem prover (ATP) attempts to discharge all POs. If all succeed, the refinement commits to Si+1. If any PO fails, the ATP produces the failing proof state (e.g., an unsatisfied VC or counterexample model), which is fed back to the LLM. The LLM may revise the code, select a different refinement rule, or backtrack to the last verified state. This yields a search-and-repair refinement process jointly guided by symbolic reasoning and neural generation.

def sqrt_w_err(N, e, max_iter=10000):
    if e <= 0 or N < 0:
        raise ValueError
    if N == 0: return 0.0
    x = N if N >= 1 else 1.0
    for _ in range(max_iter):
       x_next = 0.5 * (x + N / x)
       if (abs(x_next - x) <= e
           or abs(x_next^2 - N) <= e):
           return x_next
       x = x_next
    return x

Back to the square root example, our method generated the code below. Our code is guaranteed correct with respect to the proof obligations required by the refinement calculus in each step. Only one human input remains: This method requires the specification in first-order logic at the starting point, but not every programmer is knowledgeable in logic.

N, e = input()
x, y = 0, N+1
while y > x+e:
    if (x+y)/2*(x+y)/2 > N:
       y = (x+y)/2
    else: x = (x+y)/2

LLM-based autoformalization can mitigate this, as done in the previous case study, but the core issue remains: What if the translation is wrong? We argue that no perfect and fully automatic solution exists, as verification ultimately depends on correctness criteria defined by the user. In the experiment, our method improves the pass rate on popular datasets, such as HumanEval5 and EvalPlus,16 over the base LLM. That is, if the LLM becomes more intelligent, our method’s result will be improved on top of that. More importantly, unlike LLMs, whose pass rate decreases with more test cases, indicating that potential bugs still exist, our method’s pass rate is consistent regardless of test cases because programs are proven correct. Those that fail do so mainly because the theorem prover timed out, which, in turn, could be enhanced by LLMs.

Mitigating Autoformalization Risk

A common issue across LLM+FM paradigms is the translation from informal user intention to formal specification. We generally assume that the user sufficiently specifies their requirements in natural language and manually confirms the formal specification generated by the autoformalization module. Beyond syntax, the main risk is semantic under-specification: Natural language omits assumptions, scopes, and constraints, so an autoformalizer can produce a logically consistent but intent-misaligned specification that still passes solver checks and yields certificates for the wrong target. Robustness can be improved with typed intermediate representations and constrained decoding, where the LLM emits a type-checked schema compiled deterministically into the target formalism, and with semantic validation via round-trip paraphrases and automatically generated “should/should-not” scenarios checked against both the original intent and the formal solver.

A practical mitigation is N-version autoformalization: Generate multiple independent formalizations using different LLMs or prompt/decoding variants of the same LLM, and filter them with lightweight formal checks (well-formedness/type constraints, satisfiability and non-triviality, and consistency against fixed background constraints). Material disagreement in structure or consequences is treated as a high-risk signal and surfaced explicitly rather than being silently resolved. When appropriate, a router+specialists strategy (a system-level mixture of experts) can further reduce mismatch by dispatching inputs to domain- and logic-specific formalizers or templates, while keeping the same certificate-producing back end as the acceptance gate.

Finally, while certificate-producing back ends provide strong guarantees of logical validity, they do not eliminate epistemic uncertainty regarding specification fidelity. Formal methods act as verifiers of consistency, not arbiters of semantic truth. Bridging the informal-formal gap therefore remains an open research challenge, requiring improved interactive specification protocols, structure-aware validation, and human-in-the-loop confirmation mechanisms.

Conclusion and Future Work

This article presents a neural-symbolic paradigm in which LLMs propose candidate artifacts and formal methods gate acceptance with machine-checkable certificates. The three case studies illustrate this paradigm, but the key contribution is a reusable design view: Select from the assurance target outward, choose an FM back end for the property class, and use formal feedback to drive revision so errors become observable rather than implicit.

Beyond the case studies, the same paradigm applies to other integrations of LLMs and FM24 and applications in compliance analysis, protocol verification, cyber-physical safety, and synthesis of critical components. Recent progress around Lean further illustrates this opportunity. Mathlib17 shows how an extensive machine-checked library can support large-scale formalization and provide a strong foundation for later AI-assisted proof tools, while CSLib1 seeks to extend this effort to computer science concepts and verified code for AI-aided FM. Together, these projects suggest that shared formal libraries and reusable proof artifacts can help LLMs and formal methods achieve results beyond what either could readily do alone.

Future work will broaden these directions and further close the autoformalization gap via N-version translation (across models or prompt variants), router+specialists, typed intermediate representations, and scenario-based semantic validation.
